newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals--Cobalt firm, market eyes Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals--Cobalt firm, market eyes Zaire talks.

text.p: Cobalt prices remained strong over Japan's quiet "Golden Week" holiday season as the market waited with bated breath for news from forthcoming talks between Zaire's president and rebel leader, Asian traders said on Friday.
"Until (Zaire's President) Mobutu (Sese Seko) goes, the market remains uncertain. We're watching Zaire very carefully," said one trader at a major Japanese trading house.

On Friday Mobutu is expected to hold the first face-to-face peace talks on a ship off the Congolese coast with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who has insisted the embattled president must stand down after more than three decades in power.

A civil war in Zaire, the world's largest cobalt producer, has helped push up the metal's prices. Also contributing to higher prices is the suspension of U.S. stockpile cobalt sales due to a legal dispute between the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) and Minor Metals Inc.
"The price has overshot. But given this momentum, it could rise to about $27 (a lb)," said another trader.
Traders in Tokyo said high grade cobalt was quoted above $25 per lb and might climb further towards $30 before easing in the third quarter.

The DLA is expected to resume cobalt sales next quarter and will probably offer about 2,000 tonnes by the end of September to make up for the delay, they said. So far, it has sold only 90 tonnes in January and 500 tonnes in February.

Some traders said other main high-grade cobalt makers Inco Ltd and Falconbridge Ltd might increase their output by then, after suspending spot sales late in March when they were sold out of the metal.

Asked about Zambian cobalt, one trader said some shipments to Asia had been delayed as Zambia's monthly production fell to 350 to 360 tonnes from its planned 400 tonnes, while orders for Zambian metal surged due to uncertainties in Zaire.
In the molybdenum market prices remained strong, with further rises expected in the short term against a backdrop of strong Japanese demand, traders said.

A trader at a Japanese trade house estimated domestic demand was up about five percent from the same period a year earlier as the automobile industry enjoyed good business and a cheap yen helped other industries, such as shipmakers, win large contracts abroad.

"The strength will continue for a while, although the price should stabilise or soften in the long term," he said, adding that additional supply from Molycorp of the United States may ease the tightness in the market.
In the Asian antimony market, Chinese antimony was easy to source below $2,200 per tonne CIF (cost, insurance and freight) basis Rotterdam, a European trader in Hong Kong said.
The trader was not willing to buy, however, as he expected prices to fall further, below $2,000 and possibly to $1,900.

Official Chinese control of the antimony trade seemed to have disintegrated to some extent, he said, as some Chinese suppliers were now able to move their material to ports where they could negotiate export taxes normally around 20 percent.
Another Hong Kong trader said she had heard that quantities of up to 1,000 tonnes of antimony had moved out of China, but she had been unable to confirm the talk.
In the magnesium market, the price continued its slow advance as China was cutting output, traders said.
They agreed prices would eventually, although probably not this year, reach the $2,600 to $2,700 per tonne level, which should cover the metal's production costs in China.
Bismuth on the free market was quoted at $3.20/3.50 a lb in Rotterdam warehouses.
